newsitem.title: UK: Reuters experts too cautious on Labour win margin.
newsitem.headline: Reuters experts too cautious on Labour win margin.

text.p: Leading political analysts in a panel compiled by Reuters to predict the outcome of Britain's election hugely underestimated the scale of Labour's landslide victory, underlining an astonishing outcome.

"It's just breathtaking, the size of the Labour majority," said panellist John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester. "We haven't seen a result like that this century and I doubt very much I will ever see such a night of spectacular change."
In a final survey published on Wednesday, the average forecast was for Labour to win with a 92-seat majority. Nineteen out of 20 experts forecast a Labour win and one a hung parliament.
Election results were still being announced on Friday morning, with ITN television forecasting the final outcome as a 179-seat Labour majority in the new 659-place Parliament.
Oxford University's David Butler, the "father" of psephology, the study of elections, came closest to this with his 153-seat majority prediction.

The 20-man Reuters panel of Britain's leading political analysts, many of whom featured on election night analysis programmes, were astounded by the massive number of seats won by the Labour party, which vastly outstripped their cautious predictions.

"All along I thought this was probably going to happen but I hadn't the courage to go this far out on a limb," said Butler, who had asked Reuters to keep his forecasts unattributable. "When one makes a prediction in this sort of area and it comes out right there may be some sense behind it but there's a great deal of luck."
"One must be terribly humble about it -- it's only a game," he said.

John Curtice from Strathclyde University led the pack for months with the highest forecasts for a Labour majority. He was nearer the mark in the April 23 survey, when the panel was contacted weekly, when he predicted a 179-seat Labour majority, bang in line with the current forecast final outcome.
But in the final week Curtice eased his expectations to 131 at a time when the public opinion polls showed no sign of the Conservatives catching up with Labour.

John Benyon, whose final prediction was near the top of the range at a 143-seat majority, noted that even former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher only gained a 140-seat majority at the height of her popularity.

The analysts said they had adjusted their results downwards to account for what they called "furtive" Conservative voters as well as the risk of a debacle like 1992 when the Conservatives returned to office against the predictions of the opinion polls.
"I believe the polls tried very hard not to make the same mistakes as last time. They ended up with a pretty fair spread," said Butler.

Sydney Elliot, senior lecturer at Queen's University Belfast, predicted a seat majority of just 67, but he stressed that the experts' forecasts fell down when translating votes into seats in Britain's first-past-the-post voting system.
The average predicted percentage shares of the vote in the final Reuters survey were 34 percent for the Conservatives and 44 percent for Labour -- a 10 point lead.

The average prediction for the Liberal Democrat share of the vote was just one off at 16 percent versus 17 percent in the real poll. But on Friday Paddy Ashdown's third-placed party look set to take over 50 seats in the next parliament against 26 predicted by the panel.

"The biggest surprise is the quantity of seats, for Labour and the Liberal Democrats. There was a substantial amount of tactical voting. I was probably cautious, but if you look at the share of the vote, it's not a million miles away from the actual result," Elliot said.
Reuters first asked political scientists and pollsters in October 1996 to predict the election outcome in a monthly survey.
